prompt: An application deleted records through `GET /delete?id=7` links. After the site was indexed, several records vanished with nobody having clicked anything. What explains it?
hint: Who besides a person follows the links on a page? And what promise does the `GET` method make to whoever follows them?

choices.text: `GET` promises to change nothing, so crawlers and prefetchers repeat it freely — and every visit carried out the deletion.
choices.why: The promise is not a formality: browsers, proxies and search engines rely on it.

choices.text: The search engine sent `DELETE` to the addresses it found, following the REST convention.
choices.why: Crawlers only issue `GET`; none of them sends `DELETE` on its own initiative.

choices.text: Indexing exposed the addresses, and people visited them manually.
choices.why: That may have happened too, but the cause that explains deletions with no click is the automatic repetition of the `GET`.

choices.text: The `200` returned by the deletion made the search engine repeat the request to confirm.
choices.why: A `200` does not ask for a repeat; the crawler repeats because `GET` is declared safe, whatever the status.

prompt: Match each status code to what it communicates. There are options left over in the right-hand column.
hint: Two of them talk about identity and permission, and the difference between them is whether the server already knows who you are.

pairs.right: It has moved address for good
I do not know who you are
I know who you are, and you cannot

right_distractors: The content has not changed since last time
The request is malformed and could not be interpreted

prompt: Tick everything TLS delivers on an HTTPS connection.
hint: There are three guarantees, and one of them is what the padlock in the bar really stands for. Think too about what the network can still observe.

choices.text: Confidentiality: nobody along the path reads the content.
choices.why: It is the most remembered guarantee, and only one of the three.

choices.text: Integrity: altering the content in transit gives itself away.
choices.why: Without it, encrypting would not be enough — you could corrupt without reading.

choices.text: Authenticity: the certificate proves that server owns the domain.
choices.why: It is what the padlock stands for — "this really is the site whose name is in the bar", not "trustworthy site".

choices.text: Anonymity: the network cannot discover which domain was visited.
choices.why: The domain name and the volume of data stay visible to the network.

choices.text: Trustworthiness: the site was verified as reputable by an authority.
choices.why: The authority certifies ownership of the domain, not the honesty of whoever operates it.
